ideas.title: Foldable tray
ideas.originalProblem: Our project is a foldable tray.
ideas.originalSolution: Our oval tray has three round spaces and a central fold.
ideas.improvedProblem: If carrying or storing a tray is difficult, the user needs a tray that fits that task. We need to find out which part is awkward.
ideas.reason: Choose a real task first. This lets us check whether folding helps instead of judging the shape alone.

changes.change: Add a separate hinge pin
changes.why: The two halves can turn in a controlled way.

changes.change: Next design step: add an open stop
changes.why: Draw where contact faces would meet so the tray cannot open too far.

ideas.howItWorks: The central hinge lets the two halves fold. The drawing shows the tray shape and hinge; an open stop and any closure still need to be designed and checked before carrying objects.
printedParts: Open stop and closure still to design
suppliedParts: Measured hinge pin or suitable fastener
ideas.boundary: Use an empty model on a flat surface until the stop and closure have been designed and checked by a teacher. Use light dummy objects only. This is not a food-contact test.
test: Use this comparison: An ordinary tray carrying the same light objects.
Try opening, using and storing both trays five times. Keep the objects, route and storage place the same.
Record what happened, or write the test plan if the equipment is not available. Explain one next change.
ideas.measure: Plan how to count spills and accidental closures after a teacher checks the stop. Compare storage space.

ideas.title: Rolling bin
ideas.originalProblem: People keep littering.
ideas.originalSolution: A bin with a peaked lid rolls on wheels, with a smaller wheeled companion. It brings a place for rubbish closer to the person.
ideas.improvedProblem: A person far from a bin needs an easy place to put rubbish instead of leaving it behind.
ideas.reason: This lets us compare convenience with an ordinary nearby bin.

changes.change: Add a handle and wheel stops
changes.why: A person can move the bin and park it without it rolling away.

changes.change: Keep a wide opening
changes.why: Clean practice scraps can go in without aiming at a small hole.

ideas.boundary: Move it by hand on a clear floor. Do not claim it drives itself.
test: Compare collecting ten clean paper scraps with a parked rolling bin and an ordinary nearby bin. Count leftovers and the distance walked.
ideas.question: Does moving the bin help more than placing an ordinary bin nearby?

activities.title: Improve the problem
activities.goal: Name a person, one difficult step and the evidence we need.
steps: Read the problem statement and the suggested wording.
Ask someone what they would carry in the tray and where they would put it away.
Choose one difficult step. Complete your own improved statement.
questions: Who will use the tray, and what will they carry?
Which is difficult now: carrying, using or storing it?
Would a plain tray already solve that difficulty?
activities.successCheck: The statement names who needs help and what is difficult without promising an unproved result.

activities.title: Make the idea work
activities.goal: Show a useful change and explain how the parts connect.
steps: Show the tray open and folded.
Draw where you would add faces to stop it opening too far.
Decide whether it needs a latch and show how it would open.
questions: What will stop the tray opening too far?
Can the latch be reached without fingers entering the hinge?
Which size comes from measuring the actual practice objects?
activities.successCheck: The drawing shows an input, movement or action, and a result. It distinguishes the printed structure from supplied equipment.

activities.title: Test and explain
activities.goal: Compare fairly and explain what the result means.
steps: Use this comparison: An ordinary tray carrying the same light objects.
Try opening, using and storing both trays five times. Keep the objects, route and storage place the same.
Record what happened, or write the test plan if the equipment is not available. Explain one next change.
questions: What will we keep the same?
What result will we count or observe?
What would make us keep, change or reject the added feature?
activities.successCheck: Five opening and closing cycles without jamming, with the tray reaching a level stop each time; keep the fold only if storage improves without making use harder.

ideas.title: Mushroom lamp
ideas.originalProblem: Elderly people tend to fall when they get out of bed at night
ideas.originalSolution: Our mushroom lamp turns on when someone sits up. We drew several shapes and proposed magnetic charging.
ideas.improvedProblem: An older person getting out of bed at night needs to see the nearby floor before standing up.
ideas.reason: This names the person and the useful task. We can compare floor visibility and control use without claiming the lamp prevents falls.

changes.change: Use a wider, low base
changes.why: It may rock less in the chosen position.

changes.change: Expose a person-motion sensor and add a simple ON/OFF button
changes.why: The input and the way to stop the system are clear.

changes.change: Try a removable cap lip
changes.why: It may direct light towards the floor and reduce direct glare.

ideas.howItWorks: When ON is enabled, a real person-motion sensor signals a controller to light an LED. OFF disables it. The printed cap, stem and base support the modules; a matched bought adapter supplies low-voltage power.
suppliedParts: Matched bought wall adapter and cable
ideas.boundary: An adult selects and connects compatible low-voltage equipment. Pupils do not open an adapter or build mains wiring. A prop-motion IMU is not a stationary person-motion sensor.
test: Use this comparison: The same light at the same position without the added cap lip; include an existing nightlight if available.
Compare the two versions from a safe seated position. Try five movements in front of the stationary lamp and check OFF.
Record what happened, or write the test plan if the equipment is not available. Explain one next change.
ideas.measure: Record floor-symbol visibility, direct view of the LED, successful activations and rocking.

ideas.title: Sorting robot bin
ideas.originalProblem: Everyone is throwing things in the wrong bin.
ideas.originalSolution: The original robot bin directs items to several compartments. This two-category practice version tests the guiding movement after a person chooses a category.
ideas.improvedProblem: A person with one confusing item needs to know which local bin it belongs in.
ideas.reason: We can test an actual sorting decision instead of assuming a sensor knows every material.

changes.change: Add clear compartment labels
changes.why: People can check where an item will go.

changes.change: Use a person-operated selector first
changes.why: The movement can be tested without pretending the model recognises materials.

ideas.boundary: Use clean, dry practice items. Keep fingers out of moving parts.
test: Use five clean sample items and teacher-checked bin rules. Choose a compartment, move the guide and count items reaching the intended space.
ideas.question: What information does the bin need before it can choose the right compartment?

activities.title: Improve the problem
activities.goal: Name a person, one difficult step and the evidence we need.
steps: Read the problem statement and the suggested wording.
Ask which step is difficult at the actual bedside: seeing the floor, reaching a control or avoiding glare.
Choose one difficult step. Complete your own improved statement.
questions: Where would the lamp stand, and what floor area must be visible?
What does a motion nightlight already do?
Which single change would make this placement easier to use?
activities.successCheck: The statement names who needs help and what is difficult without promising an unproved result.

activities.title: Make the idea work
activities.goal: Show a useful change and explain how the parts connect.
steps: Mark the sensor facing the person and keep it uncovered.
Draw the light path towards the floor and the rear cable route.
Label ON/OFF and the separate bought adapter.
questions: Could the cap hide the sensor?
Does the wider base actually stay steady with its cable attached?
Can a person find and switch OFF the lamp easily?
activities.successCheck: The drawing shows an input, movement or action, and a result. It distinguishes the printed structure from supplied equipment.

activities.title: Test and explain
activities.goal: Compare fairly and explain what the result means.
steps: Use this comparison: The same light at the same position without the added cap lip; include an existing nightlight if available.
Compare the two versions from a safe seated position. Try five movements in front of the stationary lamp and check OFF.
Record what happened, or write the test plan if the equipment is not available. Explain one next change.
questions: What will we keep the same?
What result will we count or observe?
What would make us keep, change or reject the added feature?
activities.successCheck: Keep the lip only if the floor stays visible, glare improves for the observer and sensing is no worse. OFF must remain off during movement.

ideas.title: Sound companion
ideas.originalProblem: A person living alone wants something warm to hold, a sound to hear and an easy way to reach family.
ideas.originalSolution: Our cat sings when patted and sends Hello through its paw.
ideas.improvedProblem: A person living alone needs an easy way to hear a chosen sound and send a hello to family.
ideas.reason: Choose one clear action and one person. A sound or hello can be demonstrated separately from a live conversation.

changes.change: Try a clear sound button instead of patting
changes.why: Compare this change with the original pat-to-sing action and see which is easier.

changes.change: Give the heart and paw different jobs
changes.why: The person can learn one control for sound and one for hello.

changes.change: Make start and stop explicit
changes.why: The user can choose when sound plays.

ideas.howItWorks: The heart operates a switch that starts or stops a selected tune. A paw switch sends a short radio message to a second nearby board. The receiver can play a brief acknowledgement sound.
printedParts: Guides behind heart and paw controls
suppliedParts: Speaker or board with sound output
ideas.boundary: Short radio messages do not create a remote voice conversation or AI companion. Use teacher-prepared low-voltage electronics and a willing tester.
test: Use this comparison: A simple sound button with the same tune, and an ordinary hello message.
Ask a willing person to start and stop the sound without hints. Send five nearby hello messages and count acknowledgements.
Record what happened, or write the test plan if the equipment is not available. Explain one next change.
ideas.measure: Count correct first actions, accidental presses and received messages.

ideas.title: Parcel box
ideas.originalProblem: Parcels left outside the door can be taken by other people.
ideas.originalSolution: A box holds a parcel under an angled cover, with a string, pole and lock.
ideas.improvedProblem: A person receiving a parcel needs a clear way to place it inside and collect it again.
ideas.reason: We can check access and closing before making a claim about security.

changes.change: Give the cover a clear hinge and stop
changes.why: It opens in a controlled way without falling backwards.

changes.change: Keep the lock easy to reach
changes.why: The owner can practise opening and closing without reaching inside the hinge.

ideas.boundary: Use a dummy parcel and a teacher-checked model. This test does not prove theft resistance.
test: Compare an ordinary box with this cover using the same dummy parcel. Try placing, closing, unlocking and retrieving it five times.
ideas.question: How does the delivery person put a parcel in, and how does the owner get it out?

activities.title: Improve the problem
activities.goal: Name a person, one difficult step and the evidence we need.
steps: Read the problem statement and the suggested wording.
Ask a willing person what sound they would enjoy and how they would expect to stop it.
Choose one difficult step. Complete your own improved statement.
questions: Who wants this sound, and at what moment?
Do they want a recording, a hello signal or a real conversation?
What can the class actually demonstrate?
activities.successCheck: The statement names who needs help and what is difficult without promising an unproved result.

activities.title: Make the idea work
activities.goal: Show a useful change and explain how the parts connect.
steps: Show the soft outside and the removable cradle inside.
Trace heart press to sound and paw press to the nearby receiver.
Label how to stop the sound.
questions: Can the user tell the controls apart by touch?
Can the fabric press a switch accidentally?
How will the electronics be removed for care of the sleeve?
activities.successCheck: The drawing shows an input, movement or action, and a result. It distinguishes the printed structure from supplied equipment.

activities.title: Test and explain
activities.goal: Compare fairly and explain what the result means.
steps: Use this comparison: A simple sound button with the same tune, and an ordinary hello message.
Ask a willing person to start and stop the sound without hints. Send five nearby hello messages and count acknowledgements.
Record what happened, or write the test plan if the equipment is not available. Explain one next change.
questions: What will we keep the same?
What result will we count or observe?
What would make us keep, change or reject the added feature?
activities.successCheck: The person can start and stop the sound and explain the paw action; record all five hello attempts, including any missed messages.

ideas.title: Plant care
ideas.originalProblem: People are busy and forget to water their plants.
ideas.originalSolution: Our pot stores rain or wasted water and is meant to water a plant when its soil is dry. The class test uses clean water.
ideas.improvedProblem: A busy plant owner needs a way to keep a plant watered when a watering is missed.
ideas.reason: Start with the plant, pot and missed interval. Then look for an extra difficulty that an ordinary self-watering pot leaves.

changes.change: Use a bought clear reservoir
changes.why: The stored water and refill level are visible.

changes.change: Guide one continuous wick from water into soil
changes.why: The water path can be explained and checked.

changes.change: Add an open side-access wick guide
changes.why: The owner may be able to inspect or reseat the exposed wick without moving the plant.

ideas.howItWorks: A cotton wick links the water reservoir to the soil. The printed insert supports the plant above the water. The open-sided guide moves away from the wick for inspection while the wick stays in place.
printedParts: Pot insert sized to the reservoir
suppliedParts: Planting medium and practice plant or test pot
ideas.boundary: A wick is not an electronic dry-soil sensor. A short lesson cannot prove long-term plant health. Use clean water; the printed part does not need to be the leak-tight reservoir.
test: Use this comparison: A plain wick reservoir with the same container, wick and planting medium.
For class, demonstrate the path and compare access to the wick. Plan a longer water-delivery comparison with equal starting water and conditions.
Record what happened, or write the test plan if the equipment is not available. Explain one next change.
ideas.measure: Count steps or disturbance needed to inspect the wick. Later measure water delivered or reservoir change over an agreed interval.

ideas.title: Doorbell wristband
ideas.originalProblem: People with hearing difficulties may not hear the doorbell at home.
ideas.originalSolution: A wristband flashes and vibrates when the doorbell rings.
ideas.improvedProblem: A person who misses a doorbell needs an alert they can notice where they usually sit or move.
ideas.reason: The useful result is noticing the visitor, so we can compare different cues.

changes.change: Provide separate light and vibration cues
changes.why: The person can choose which cue they notice best.

changes.change: Use an adjustable strap and reachable control
changes.why: The band can fit comfortably and be easy to check.

ideas.boundary: An adult checks the separate receiver, battery and vibration parts. Waterproofing has not been tested.
test: With a willing person, compare five agreed light or vibration cues in a quiet role-play. Record noticed and missed cues.
ideas.question: Which cue does the person notice best, and where will they wear or keep it?

activities.title: Improve the problem
activities.goal: Name a person, one difficult step and the evidence we need.
steps: Read the problem statement and the suggested wording.
Ask what actually goes wrong when watering is missed, and whether checking or refilling an existing reservoir is difficult.
Choose one difficult step. Complete your own improved statement.
questions: Which plant and pot are we helping?
What does an ordinary wick pot already solve?
Is seeing or reaching the wick a real remaining difficulty?
activities.successCheck: The statement names who needs help and what is difficult without promising an unproved result.

activities.title: Make the idea work
activities.goal: Show a useful change and explain how the parts connect.
steps: Trace one unbroken wick from below the water surface into the soil.
Show a gap between stored water and the pot floor.
Show the guide moving sideways without pulling out the buried wick.
questions: Does the lower wick stay in the water as the level drops?
Can the guide come off without breaking the water path?
Where can water be added without spilling into the wrong place?
activities.successCheck: The drawing shows an input, movement or action, and a result. It distinguishes the printed structure from supplied equipment.

activities.title: Test and explain
activities.goal: Compare fairly and explain what the result means.
steps: Use this comparison: A plain wick reservoir with the same container, wick and planting medium.
For class, demonstrate the path and compare access to the wick. Plan a longer water-delivery comparison with equal starting water and conditions.
Record what happened, or write the test plan if the equipment is not available. Explain one next change.
questions: What will we keep the same?
What result will we count or observe?
What would make us keep, change or reject the added feature?
activities.successCheck: Keep the guide only if inspection is easier and the wick remains connected. The longer trial must show suitable delivery for the chosen pot without overflow.

ideas.title: Parcel notice
ideas.originalProblem: Our topic is parcels at the door.
ideas.originalSolution: Our topic is parcels left at the door. This parcel notice is a starting idea to discuss.
ideas.improvedProblem: A parcel recipient needs to notice a delivery when the usual knock or message is missed.
ideas.reason: A real example can show whether notice is the difficulty, rather than storage, collection or security.

changes.change: Make the input a guided pressure plate
changes.why: A dummy parcel can produce a visible, repeatable movement.

changes.change: Use a switch and nearby radio receiver
changes.why: The arrival can be signalled at a different place.

changes.change: Keep an icon until acknowledgement
changes.why: A short signal can leave a reminder for the recipient to check.

ideas.howItWorks: The parcel lowers a spring-returned plate onto a microswitch. A controller sends a short message. The receiver shows an icon until its acknowledgement button is pressed.
ideas.boundary: This is a tabletop arrival demonstration, not theft prevention or a weatherproof doormat. An adult prepares the electronics and selects the spring.
test: Use this comparison: An ordinary knock or message in the same pretend delivery routine.
Use five dummy deliveries. A tester at the receiver acknowledges each alert. Include a light parcel and a parcel left in place.
Record what happened, or write the test plan if the equipment is not available. Explain one next change.
ideas.measure: Count deliveries noticed, repeated alerts and plate resets.

ideas.title: Crossing the road
ideas.originalProblem: Our topic is crossing the road.
ideas.originalSolution: A reminder cuff is one idea to discuss. The group still needs to explain its own drawing.
ideas.improvedProblem: A person approaching a crossing needs to remember the safe steps taught by an adult.
ideas.reason: This gives us one small reminder task to discuss without claiming a device makes traffic safe.

changes.change: Use a short readable reminder
changes.why: The person can explain the message in their own words.

changes.change: Make the message face the wearer
changes.why: It can be read without twisting the wrist.

ideas.boundary: This is a classroom discussion. Do not test in live traffic or rely on the cuff for road safety.
test: Use a paper road scene indoors. Ask a pupil to explain the reminder and choose what to do next. Compare with an ordinary instruction card.
ideas.question: What does your original small drawing show, and who would use your idea?

activities.title: Improve the problem
activities.goal: Name a person, one difficult step and the evidence we need.
steps: Read the problem statement and the suggested wording.
Ask a recipient to describe a missed parcel notice and the method they use now.
Choose one difficult step. Complete your own improved statement.
questions: Was the notice missed, or was collecting the parcel difficult?
Where must the alert be noticed?
What should happen if a parcel stays on the plate?
activities.successCheck: The statement names who needs help and what is difficult without promising an unproved result.

activities.title: Make the idea work
activities.goal: Show a useful change and explain how the parts connect.
steps: Show the plate above the switch and the spring returning it.
Draw a radio arrow to the separate receiver.
Label who presses acknowledge and what that changes.
questions: Will a light parcel move the plate enough?
What stops repeated alerts from one delivery?
Can the parcel be removed without trapping the plate?
activities.successCheck: The drawing shows an input, movement or action, and a result. It distinguishes the printed structure from supplied equipment.

activities.title: Test and explain
activities.goal: Compare fairly and explain what the result means.
steps: Use this comparison: An ordinary knock or message in the same pretend delivery routine.
Use five dummy deliveries. A tester at the receiver acknowledges each alert. Include a light parcel and a parcel left in place.
Record what happened, or write the test plan if the equipment is not available. Explain one next change.
questions: What will we keep the same?
What result will we count or observe?
What would make us keep, change or reject the added feature?
activities.successCheck: Each agreed test parcel should produce one clear arrival event; acknowledgement clears the reminder, and removal lets the plate reset.

ideas.title: Drone response
ideas.originalProblem: There is a fire. A fire scanner alerts drones.
ideas.originalSolution: Our drone is meant to help put out a fire and search for people with a light. This drawing develops the light and operator link. We still need to explain how it would put out the fire.
ideas.improvedProblem: A rescue team needs clear information about a place that is difficult to see or reach.
ideas.reason: This names the information the drone should help gather before choosing its equipment.

changes.change: Show the drone and its search light
changes.why: The drawing explains the flying response idea.

changes.change: Show what the operator needs to know
changes.why: The group can explain the message and the next action.

ideas.howItWorks: A detector sends an alert. The group explains how an operator directs the drone, uses its light and receives information. Equipment and mechanism choices remain to be confirmed.
printedParts: Possible housing or light mount, only after checking the selected drone
suppliedParts: Suitable drone and controller selected by a qualified adult
Compatible light and communication equipment if needed
ideas.boundary: This is a design discussion, not a flight or fire test. A qualified adult must check any real drone, equipment and safe operating location.
test: Compare a clear location message with a vague message in an indoor role-play.
Use pretend messages and a paper plan indoors.
Record which messages let the receiver identify the right place.
ideas.measure: Count which messages let the listener identify the correct place on a paper plan.

ideas.title: Detect and alert
ideas.originalProblem: A fire scanner detects a problem and alerts the drone.
ideas.originalSolution: The scanner detects a fire, alerts the drone and is meant to show people a way out. This drawing develops the alert and location message. We still need to explain the projected guidance.
ideas.improvedProblem: A person receiving an alert needs to know what happened and where help is needed.
ideas.reason: The message can be checked before claiming a reliable detection system.

changes.change: Include a location in the alert
changes.why: The receiver knows which place to check.

changes.change: Show the receiver and its next action
changes.why: The group can explain the link from detection to drone response.

ideas.boundary: Do not use fire, heat, smoke or powder. The detector and drone functions still need real equipment and adult checks.
test: Use five pretend alert cards and a paper plan. Compare messages with and without locations. Record whether the receiver chooses the right place.
ideas.question: What detects the problem, who receives the message, and what happens next?

activities.title: Improve the problem
activities.goal: Name a person, one difficult step and the evidence we need.
steps: Read the drone response and detection sections.
Name who needs the information and where.
Explain what the drone should help them see or learn.
questions: Who receives the alert?
What information is missing?
Who controls the drone?
activities.successCheck: The statement names who needs help and what is difficult without promising an unproved result.

activities.title: Make the idea work
activities.goal: Show a useful change and explain how the parts connect.
steps: Draw the drone and the light.
Label what it receives and what it sends back.
Explain who controls it and how it stops.
questions: What does the drone help someone see?
What message does it receive?
Who decides its next action?
activities.successCheck: The drawing shows an input, movement or action, and a result. It distinguishes the printed structure from supplied equipment.

activities.title: Test and explain
activities.goal: Compare fairly and explain what the result means.
steps: Compare a clear location message with a vague message in an indoor role-play.
Use pretend messages and a paper plan indoors.
Record which messages let the receiver identify the right place.
questions: What will we keep the same?
What result will we count or observe?
What would make us keep, change or reject the added feature?
activities.successCheck: The receiver identifies the intended place from the message. This checks communication only, not flight or fire response.

ideas.title: Recycling reasons quiz
ideas.originalProblem: People not knowing what goes in which bin.
ideas.originalSolution: Our quiz helps people choose which bin to use.
ideas.improvedProblem: People using a shared bin need help to check a confusing item before dropping it in.
ideas.reason: A correct answer and a reason show more understanding than recognising a familiar picture.

changes.change: Keep one item and change its condition
changes.why: The learner can see why the next action may change.

changes.change: Hide the reason behind a sliding cover
changes.why: The learner makes a choice before looking.

changes.change: Add guide rails and retaining stops
changes.why: The moving parts stay aligned and attached.

ideas.howItWorks: A manual slider selects the item condition. A separate cover reveals the matching paper reason row after the learner chooses an answer. Teacher-approved paper cards contain the recycling rules.
ideas.boundary: The model is a manual learning aid. It does not recognise real rubbish. The teacher checks every local rule and example.
test: Use this comparison: Ordinary recycling rule cards with the same information.
After trying each method, use five new teacher-approved examples. Ask for the action and the reason, not only a score.
Record what happened, or write the test plan if the equipment is not available. Explain one next change.
ideas.measure: Count correct actions and explanations on unfamiliar examples; note slider jams.

ideas.title: Bin feedback
ideas.originalProblem: People keep throwing things in the wrong bin.
ideas.originalSolution: A bin gives red or green feedback about a sorting choice.
ideas.improvedProblem: A person with a confusing item needs to understand why it belongs in a particular bin.
ideas.reason: An explanation helps the person make the next choice as well.

changes.change: Show a reason with each colour
changes.why: The user learns what was right or wrong.

changes.change: Use a teacher-controlled choice first
changes.why: The feedback can be tried before adding any unproved item sensor.

ideas.boundary: A coloured light does not identify a material by itself. Use clean practice items.
test: Use five clean items with teacher-checked rules. Give a word or symbol as well as colour, then ask the person to explain the choice.
ideas.question: How will someone understand the feedback if they cannot tell the colours apart?

questions: Which one item will stay the same?
What condition changes the decision?
What reason should the learner explain?
activities.successCheck: The statement names who needs help and what is difficult without promising an unproved result.

activities.goal: Show a useful change and explain how the parts connect.
steps: Show the same-item card and two condition positions.
Use separate arrows for changing condition and revealing the reason.
Mark where the sliders stop so they stay in their rails.
questions: Can the cover reveal the correct row without showing the answer early?
Do the stops keep the slider attached?
Can the paper card be changed without rebuilding the whole model?
activities.successCheck: The drawing shows an input, movement or action, and a result. It distinguishes the printed structure from supplied equipment.

activities.title: Test and explain
activities.goal: Compare fairly and explain what the result means.
steps: Use this comparison: Ordinary recycling rule cards with the same information.
After trying each method, use five new teacher-approved examples. Ask for the action and the reason, not only a score.
Record what happened, or write the test plan if the equipment is not available. Explain one next change.
questions: What will we keep the same?
What result will we count or observe?
What would make us keep, change or reject the added feature?
activities.successCheck: The moving parts complete ten manual cycles without leaving their guides. Keep the extra mechanism only if it improves explanation or use compared with plain cards.

ideas.title: Reachable light control
ideas.originalProblem: The light switch is too far from the bed, and the room is dark.
ideas.originalSolution: Our round pendant has side-by-side ON and OFF controls for a light.
ideas.improvedProblem: An older person in bed needs to control the room light without getting up to reach a distant switch.
ideas.reason: The reach difficulty is specific. We can compare control use from the same comfortable position.

changes.change: Keep the round case and side-by-side controls
changes.why: The main original form remains recognisable.

changes.change: Add different raised shapes and a separating ridge
changes.why: ON and OFF may be easier to distinguish in a single-grey print.

changes.change: Guide caps onto a matched remote module
changes.why: Each press has a real path to a switch.

ideas.howItWorks: A cap presses its aligned switch on a compatible remote module. The matched receiver controls a low-voltage lamp. The printed case guides the caps and supports the module.
ideas.boundary: Tactile shapes are not automatically valid Braille. An adult pairs compatible equipment; pupils do not switch or wire mains electricity.
test: Use this comparison: The same compatible remote placed within comfortable reach.
From a safe seated position, compare finding and pressing ON/OFF with the ordinary remote and the new case.
Record what happened, or write the test plan if the equipment is not available. Explain one next change.
ideas.measure: Count correct first choices, mistaken presses and requests for help.

ideas.title: Firestructor cooking screen
ideas.originalProblem: Food is left cooking when someone walks away and forgets.
ideas.originalSolution: Firestructor shows cooking instructions and recipes on a screen.
ideas.improvedProblem: A person following a recipe needs clear instructions and a way to keep track of the current step.
ideas.reason: We can compare how clearly the steps are understood in a cold practice activity.

changes.change: Show clear steps with Next and Back controls
changes.why: The person can move through the recipe and repeat an instruction.

changes.change: Support the screen and tidy the cable
changes.why: The instructions stay readable while the lead stays out of the work area.

ideas.boundary: Do not use a hot stove. A recipe screen does not detect or stop a fire.
test: Use the same cold pretend recipe on paper and on the screen. Count missed steps and requests for help. Ask which instructions were easier to follow.
ideas.question: Which cooking step is forgotten, and what should the reminder ask the person to do?

activities.title: Improve the problem
activities.goal: Name a person, one difficult step and the evidence we need.
steps: Read the problem statement and the suggested wording.
Ask the intended user whether reaching, finding or pressing the present control is difficult.
Choose one difficult step. Complete your own improved statement.
questions: Can the ordinary remote simply be moved within reach?
How will ON and OFF feel different without relying on colour?
What size and force suit the actual person?

steps: Keep two controls side by side in a round case.
Show each cap aligned with its switch.
Draw the signal going to the matching lamp receiver.

What guides and returns each cap?

activities.title: Test and explain
activities.goal: Compare fairly and explain what the result means.
steps: Use this comparison: The same compatible remote placed within comfortable reach.
From a safe seated position, compare finding and pressing ON/OFF with the ordinary remote and the new case.
Record what happened, or write the test plan if the equipment is not available. Explain one next change.

What result will we count or observe?
What would make us keep, change or reject the added feature?

ideas.title: Phone sleep holder
ideas.originalProblem: wasting phone energy and too much screen time
ideas.originalSolution: Our phone-sized bed holder has a blanket, charging pocket, lock and custom headboard.
ideas.improvedProblem: Someone choosing a phone break needs help to stop screen use during an agreed rest period.
ideas.reason: First find the reason for pickups. Screen time and energy are different outcomes, and a holder does not prove either benefit by its shape.

changes.change: Make the blanket a guided slider
changes.why: It can cover and uncover the screen in a repeatable way.

changes.change: Next design step: add an end stop
changes.why: Decide how to keep the sliding cover attached while still letting the phone come out.

ideas.howItWorks: A card phone fits in the cradle. The blanket slides along side rails using its pull tab. An end stop and any locking mechanism still need to be designed. A separate channel leads towards the proposed charging pocket.
printedParts: Blanket slider, rails and pull tab
End stop and any lock still to design
suppliedParts: Cable for an unplugged routing check
ideas.boundary: The drawing shows a manual sliding cover, not a timed lock. Use a dummy phone first. Live charging needs separate hardware and ventilation checks. No energy saving is claimed.
test: Use this comparison: An ordinary phone parking place during the same voluntary routine.
Use a dummy first for five open/close cycles. For a voluntary behaviour comparison, count pickups and ask why each happens.
Record what happened, or write the test plan if the equipment is not available. Explain one next change.
ideas.measure: Record fit, jams, accidental release and pickup reasons.

ideas.title: Recycling mascot
ideas.originalProblem: People put the wrong things in the blue bin.
ideas.originalSolution: Two mascot designs give feedback. Correct choices earn stickers, with a keychain reward.
ideas.improvedProblem: A person sorting rubbish needs to understand a confusing item before choosing the blue bin.
ideas.reason: We can check whether the person learns the rule rather than only collecting a reward.

changes.change: Put a short reason on the screen
changes.why: The mascot explains the choice.

changes.change: Keep rewards separate from the item opening
changes.why: Stickers can be collected without reaching near the rubbish.

ideas.boundary: Use clean items and a person to select the feedback. Fake hands must not grab a person.
test: Compare explanation-only feedback with explanation plus a sticker. Then ask about new items without rewards.
ideas.question: Will the person still choose correctly when no sticker is offered?

ideas.title: Living-room caption display
ideas.originalProblem: Cannot hear clearly
ideas.originalSolution: Our caption display shows spoken words as text for a person who cannot hear clearly.
ideas.improvedProblem: A person who cannot hear speech clearly needs to follow the words in an everyday conversation.
ideas.reason: Name the conversation and person, then check whether the displayed words can be followed.

changes.change: Use a compatible device running speech-to-text software
changes.why: The proposal has a real route from speech to captions.

changes.change: Support it in a frame with a tilt hinge and stops
changes.why: The screen can be positioned for the reader.

changes.change: Try a removable shade and rear cable route
changes.why: Glare and cable interference can be compared.

ideas.howItWorks: A suitable microphone and speech-to-text app on a supplied phone or tablet produce captions. A printed frame holds the device. A hinge and stop positions change its viewing angle; a removable shade may reduce glare.
ideas.boundary: A basic micro:bit sound-level sensor measures loudness, not words. A printed frame does not produce captions. The fire-car alternative is a manual demonstration only, without fire or powder.
test: Use this comparison: The same caption device in an ordinary position or stand.
Use the same short phrases, reader position and lighting. Compare readability with two frame positions or with and without the shade.
Record what happened, or write the test plan if the equipment is not available. Explain one next change.
ideas.measure: Count important missed words and requests to reposition the screen. Separate transcription errors from visibility problems.

ideas.title: Fire response car
ideas.originalProblem: The group wants to help people with cooking or gas-related fire problems.
ideas.originalSolution: A wheeled car carries a jointed arm and a quick-release extinguisher holder.
ideas.improvedProblem: A person responding to a fire needs help reaching a dangerous area without entering it.
ideas.reason: This keeps the real need clear. The class can safely check movement and stability, while emergency functions remain untested.

changes.change: Give each joint a clear stop
changes.why: The arm has a repeatable range of movement.

changes.change: Keep the body stable while the arm moves
changes.why: We can check whether the arm makes the model tip.

ideas.boundary: Use no fire, heat, gas, powder or pressure. Do not attach a real extinguisher or claim the model is fireproof.
test: Use a hand-moved model with a lightweight dummy payload. Try five arm positions and check stability on a clear floor.
ideas.question: What keeps the car stable when its arm reaches forwards or sideways?
